why.text_en: Guten Morgen — Good morning: same idea, same order. Learn it as one block; why Guten and not gut comes in later lessons.
why.why_de_en: A ready-made wish: "(I wish you a) good morning". Germans say it as one block.
why.why_en: Just like English "Good morning!": a fixed greeting you learn as one piece. Guten Morgen — Good morning. The words are even related: gut ≈ good, Morgen ≈ morning.

why_not.en: Common mistake: Gute instead of Guten. Learn the whole block: Guten Morgen. Why it works this way comes in later lessons.

why.root_en: Morgen: Germanic *murgina-, the same root as English morning and morrow (as in tomorrow) (DWDS, Pfeifer, Wiktionary)
why.why_voice_en: Guten Morgen — Good morning: same idea, same order. Learn it as one block; why Guten and not gut comes in later lessons.

why.why_en: Like English, German needs the verb: Ich bin {hero_name} — I am {hero_name}. bin means am (not "been"). "Ich {hero_name}" is as broken as "I {hero_name}".

why_not.en: Don't drop bin: "Ich …" without bin is a fragment, just like "I …" without am. And bin means am, not "been".

why.root_en: bin, bist: from the old root *bʰew- ("be"), like English be; ist: from *es-, like English is. The verb sein is made of two roots (DWDS, Wiktionary)

ch01_t04.en: Good day, my name is Anna.

why.text_en: The greeting doesn't take a car: ich is car #1.
why.why_de_en: ich · heiße · Anna: the action heiße is car #2, the backbone of the sentence.
why.why_en: Guten Tag, ich heiße Anna — Hello, I'm called Anna. Like English, the "I" must be there: heiße alone is not enough.

why_not.en: Don't drop ich: "heiße Anna" alone is cut off, like "am called Anna" in English.

why.why_voice_en: The greeting doesn't take a car: ich is car #1.

why.text_en: der Name → dein Name (with du).
why.why_de_en: The question word Wie is car #1, the action ist comes right after it, car #2: Wie ist dein Name? A German first says WHAT he wants to know.
why.why_en: Like English "What is your name?": question word, then the verb. Wie ist dein Name? — literally "How is your name?". German asks with wie (how), not was (what).

why_not.en: dein Name went before ist, so the action left car #2. After Wie the verb comes at once, as in English "What is…".

why.root_en: ist and English is: one old root *es- (DWDS, Wiktionary); Name and English name: one old root *h₁nómn̥ (Wiktionary)
why.why_voice_en: der Name → dein Name (with du).

why.text_en: It starts with "to whom": the action is still car #2.
why.why_de_en: Car #1 is taken: mir. The action geht is still car #2, and the "who" (es) comes after it: Danke, mir geht es gut.
why.why_en: English keeps "it" before the verb; German keeps the verb in car #2. Mir geht es gut — literally "To me goes it well", meaning I'm fine.

why_not.en: English order (es geht) pushed geht to car #3. A German will understand you but will hear the mistake right away.

why.why_voice_en: It starts with "to whom": the action is still car #2.

why.text_en: der Mann = he.
why.why_de_en: The question word Wer is car #1, the action ist comes right after it, car #2: Wer ist der Mann? A German first says WHAT he wants to know.
why.why_en: Like English "Who is the man?": question word, verb, then the rest. Wer ist der Mann? — Who is the man? Careful: wer means who, not "where".

why_not.en: der Mann went before ist, so the action left car #2. After Wer the verb comes at once, as in English "Who is…".

why.root_en: ist and English is: one old root *es- (DWDS, Wiktionary)
why.why_voice_en: der Mann = he.

ch01_t08.en: This is my neighbor, Ms. Schmidt.

why.why_de_en: ist works like an "=" sign: das = meine Nachbarin, Frau Schmidt. The action holds car #2. On the right is the same "who" role, so the article doesn't change: meine Nachbarin, Frau Schmidt.
why.why_en: Like English "This is my neighbor, Ms. Schmidt": the verb is needed. Das ist meine Nachbarin — This is my neighbor. German marks a woman with -in: Nachbar → Nachbarin.

why_not.en: Don't drop ist: "Mein Name …" without ist is a fragment, just like "My name …" without the word is.

why.root_en: Nachbarin = Nachbar + -in; Nachbar and English neighbor: one old word, "near-dweller" (Wiktionary); ist and English is: one root *es- (DWDS)

why.text_en: nicht goes at the end.
why.why_de_en: nicht goes before what it negates; if the "no" is about the whole sentence, nicht moves to the end: Ich verstehe Sie nicht.
why.why_en: English puts "don't" before the verb: I don't understand you. German puts nicht at the end, with no "do": Ich verstehe Sie nicht — literally "I understand you not".

why_not.en: English order ("I don't understand") puts nicht too early. In German, nicht doesn't go before verstehe; it moves further back, usually to the end.

why.why_voice_en: nicht goes at the end.

why.text_en: Yes/no question: the action first.
why.why_de_en: The action in front (Kommst) signals a yes/no question from the very first word, even before the melody: Kommst du aus der Ukraine?
why.why_en: No "do" in German: Kommst du aus der Ukraine? — Do you come from Ukraine? The verb itself moves to the front, and with du it ends in -st.

why_not.en: Not a mistake, but it sounds different: like English "You're from Ukraine?!", it's a surprised double-check. A normal question puts the action first.

why.root_en: du and English thou (the old "you" for friends) are one old root *tū̌, like Latin tū (DWDS, Pfeifer, Wiktionary)
why.why_voice_en: Yes/no question: the action first.

why.text_en: With er/sie: kommt.
why.why_de_en: Frau Wagner · kommt · aus Dresden: the action kommt is car #2, the backbone of the sentence.
why.why_en: Like English "Ms. Wagner comes from Dresden": the verb is needed, and with one person (er/sie) it ends in -t, as English adds -s: kommt — comes.

why_not.en: Don't drop the verb: "Frau Wagner aus Dresden" is a fragment, like "Ms. Wagner from Dresden". Keep kommt.

why.why_voice_en: With er/sie: kommt.

why.text_en: The "who" comes after the action.
why.why_de_en: The question word Woher is car #1, the action kommt comes right after it, car #2: Woher kommt Herr Schmidt? A German first says WHAT he wants to know.
why.why_en: English adds "does": Where does Mr. Schmidt come from? German has no "do" and puts the verb right after the question word: Woher kommt Herr Schmidt?

why_not.en: Herr Schmidt went before kommt, so the action left car #2. After Woher a German expects the verb at once, or it's not a question.

why.why_voice_en: The "who" comes after the action.

why.text_en: With sie: wohnt.
why.why_de_en: The question word Wo is car #1, the action wohnt comes right after it, car #2: Wo wohnt Frau Wagner? A German first says WHAT he wants to know.
why.why_en: English adds "does": Where does Ms. Wagner live? German has no "do": Wo wohnt Frau Wagner? The verb comes right after Wo and ends in -t.

why_not.en: Frau Wagner went before wohnt, so the action left car #2. After Wo a German expects the verb at once, or it's not a question.

why.why_voice_en: With sie: wohnt.

why.text_en: das Dorf → in einem Dorf (where).
why.why_de_en: Wir · wohnen · in einem Dorf: the action wohnen is car #2, the backbone of the sentence.
why.why_en: Same order as English: Wir wohnen in einem Dorf — We live in a village. wohnen stays in car #2 even if you start with another word.

why_not.en: The action wohnen moved to the end. That's how the tail of a long sentence after "that" or "because" sounds; in a simple sentence wohnen is car #2.

why.why_voice_en: das Dorf → in einem Dorf (where).

why.text_en: It starts with "when", so wir comes after the action.
why.why_de_en: Car #1 is taken: Jetzt. The action wohnen is still car #2, and the "who" (wir) comes after it: Jetzt wohnen wir in Sachsen.
why.why_en: English says "Now we live in Saxony". German keeps the verb in car #2, so wir moves behind it: Jetzt wohnen wir in Sachsen — literally "Now live we in Saxony".

why_not.en: English order (Jetzt wir wohnen) pushed wohnen to car #3. A German will understand you but will hear the mistake right away.

why.why_voice_en: It starts with "when", so wir comes after the action.

ch01_t18.en: Good evening! What is your name?

why.text_en: In the evening, Guten Abend; then the same question: Wie · heißen · Sie.
why.why_de_en: The question word Wie is car #1, the action heißen comes right after it, car #2: Wie heißen Sie? A German first says WHAT he wants to know.
why.why_en: Like English "What is your name?": question word first, then the verb. Wie heißen Sie? — literally "How are you called?". German never adds "do" here.

why_not.en: Sie went before heißen, so the action left car #2. After Wie a German expects the verb at once, just as "What your name is?" sounds wrong in English.

why.why_voice_en: In the evening, Guten Abend; then the same question: Wie · heißen · Sie.

why.text_en: In the daytime, Guten Tag; the same question the neighbor asks in the evening: Ihnen means "to you".

why.why_en: English asks with "be": How are you? German uses gehen (go): Wie geht es Ihnen? — literally "How goes it to you?". The order is fixed: Wie · geht · es · Ihnen.

why_not.en: es went before geht, so the action left car #2. After Wie a German expects the verb at once, or it's not a question.

why.why_voice_en: In the daytime, Guten Tag; the same question the neighbor asks in the evening: Ihnen means "to you".

why.why_en: English asks everyone "How are you?"; German picks: Wie geht es dir? (du) — Wie geht es Ihnen? (Sie). Both are literally "How goes it to you?".

why.why_en: English says "So-so" with no verb. German needs one: Es geht so — literally "It goes so". In speech the es is often dropped: Geht so.

why_not.en: Like English "So-so" without a verb, "Es so" is only a fragment to a German. Keep geht: Es geht so.
